name: Jodï

catalog_locator: Section 3 Phonology, printed pp. 557-558 = PDF pp. 11-12 of 68 (running heads '12 Jodï 557', '558 Jorge Emilio Rosés Labrada'): Table 12.9 (p. 557), Table 12.10 (p. 558), surrounding text and footnote 11 (p. 558). File: the copy we hold.
catalog_quote: With respect to stress, Vilera Díaz (1985) makes some preliminary observations, suggesting that, while stress placement on nouns is difficult to account for, stress on demonstratives is consistently placed on the final syllable and proposing that it is also used to disambiguate cases where a noun has the same form as the demonstrative. ... In these examples, note that the nouns have different stress patterns – penult for examples (a–c) and (e) versus final stress for (f–h) – while the demonstratives always have the stress on the final syllable ... Based on this contrast, she suggests that Jodï stress may be phonemic, although she does not provide any minimal pairs other than the one in (e). Additional minimal pairs are, however, available. Quatra (2008a: 26) explains that stress is not represented in the writing system unless it is needed to disambiguate two words; his examples follow here in Table 12.10. Note that all the examples, except for the first one, are bisyllabic and that, although stress in ˈmihĩ <míji̱> ‘small calabash’ does serve to distinguish a noun from a matching demonstrative, this is not the only use of stress, as most of the pairs do not involve a contrasting noun-demonstrative pair. [Tab. 12.10, penultimate vs final stress: ˈbaba <bába> ‘father’ / baˈba <baba> ‘classifier for flat things’; ˈʰtali ‘enter’ / ʰtaˈli ‘moriche palm’; ˈbude ‘whistle (v.)’ / buˈde ‘light a fire’; ˈnuwɛ̃ ‘go back’ / nuˈwẽ ‘house, hut’]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (68 pp., text layer, published De Gruyter layout, running head "12 Jodï", DOI 10.1515/9783110419405-012 printed on p. 547). Section 3 Phonology, printed pp. 557-558 = PDF pages 11-12. Every segment of the reader's quote is there verbatim: p. 557 "With respect to stress, Vilera Díaz (1985) makes some preliminary observations, suggesting that, while stress placement on nouns is difficult to account for, stress on demonstratives is consistently placed on the final syllable and proposing that it is also used to disambiguate cases where a noun has the same form as the demonstrative.. note that the nouns have different stress patterns – penult for examples (a–c) and (e) versus final stress…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is not predictable from the segmental form: disyllabic nouns and verbs show either penultimate (initial) or final stress, and Table 12.10 (from Quatra 2008a: 26) gives nine minimal pairs contrasting penultimate vs final stress (e.g. ˈbaba 'father' vs baˈba 'classifier for flat things'; ˈbude 'whistle' vs buˈde 'light a fire'; ˈnuwɛ̃ 'go back' vs nuˈwẽ 'house'), so stress is treated as (probably) phonemic. One morphological regularity: demonstratives always carry final stress, which can disambiguate a noun from a homophonous demonstrative (ˈmĩhi 'calabash' vs mĩˈhi demonstrative+classifier). Vilera Díaz's noun examples split between penult (buˈhʷãmbo, ˈnãla, ˈbʷɛlo, ˈmĩhi) and final (nõˈnõ, doˈdo, mõʰˈto). The author states that prosody 'require[s] further research'. Contrasting earlier view: Guarisma Pinto (1974: 49) preliminarily judged stress and vowel length non-contrastive (reported in Rosés Labrada 2019, supplemental appendix p. 8, file).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. Table 12.9 (d) ˈmẽʰnãheʰˈta 'shoe' carries two stress marks (as transcribed from Vilera Díaz 1985) but the text does not comment on it.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 11 (p. 558): Quatra's orthography marks stress only in the first column of the minimal pairs; the author inferred final stress for the unmarked partners, which he notes is problematic for the trisyllabic ãmi-ˈhã 'coroba grub'. Guarisma Pinto (1974) instead claimed pre-aspiration occurs 'automatically in pre-stressed positions' and that stress is not contrastive.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms (isolated words from elicited wordlists/dictionary; no texts exist). The chapter is explicitly a philological sketch based on secondary data (Vilera Díaz 1985, Quatra 2008a/b, Guarisma Pinto 1974/1978) plus the author's listening to Mattei Müller's AILLA audio; the stress observations are taken from Vilera Díaz 1985: 38-39 and Quatra 2008a: 26.
new_statements.identity_note: Rosés Labrada 2023 covers Jodï as a whole (San José de Kayamá and Caño Iguana communities); no dialect split is described. Glottolog yuwa1244 = Hoti/Jodï; the on-disk directory hoti1237 is a different, unrelated language (name coincidence only).

readall_conflicts: The pre-existing sources already held by the project disagree among themselves: Guarisma Pinto 1974 (as reported in Rosés Labrada 2019, supplemental appendix p. 8) says preliminary analysis suggests stress and vowel length are not contrastive, whereas Vilera Díaz 1985 and Quatra 2008a (as reported in Rosés Labrada 2023: 557-558, Tables 12.9-12.10) give penult-vs-final minimal pairs (ˈbaba 'father' vs baˈba 'flat classifier', ˈbude 'whistle' vs buˈde 'light a fire', etc.) and treat stress as (possibly) phonemic, with demonstratives consistently final-stressed and noun placement 'difficult to account for'. The catalog's lexical (unpredictable) reading follows the later, better-documented sources.
